text: Odysseus and the Sirens: When Should We Ask Others Not to Obey Our Future Selves?
Odysseus knows that willpower alone cannot resist the Sirens' song.
He is neither unaware of the danger nor too late to prepare.

Circe has already told him how to pass through the Sirens' waters: the crew must stop their ears with wax and keep rowing. If Odysseus wants to listen, they must tie him to the mast. However he begs or commands, they must not untie him. Instead, they must bind the ropes tighter.
Odysseus accepts this arrangement.
As the ship approaches, he hands the wax to his companions himself and has them plug their ears. Then they bind him fast.
When the song reaches him, what the Sirens promise is not merely pleasure.
They call him by name, speak of Troy, and say they know everything that happens on earth. It is an almost irresistible invitation: come a little closer, and you will know more.
Odysseus immediately wants to go.
He frowns, signals, and orders his companions to release him.
The crew does not obey.
They bend to their rowing, and some come over to tighten the knots. Only when the song has faded and the danger has truly passed do they remove the wax from their ears and untie Odysseus.
In this story, the same person gives two conflicting commands.
The first says:
Later I will ask you to let me go. When that happens, do not listen.
The second says:
Let me go now.
Which Odysseus should the crew obey?
We usually understand “deciding for oneself” as something straightforward.
I act on what I want now. If someone stops me, they are deciding for me.
But Odysseus before the Sirens makes this more complicated.

Before hearing the song, he already knows it will change his judgment. He is not predicting that he will fall unconscious, nor imagining he will be unable to speak. Quite the opposite: he knows his future self will still give clear commands, and give them with great urgency.
What will no longer be reliable is not his voice.
It is the direction that voice serves.
Before approaching the Sirens, he wants to leave alive and also hear the song. He designs a way to accommodate both wishes: his ears can listen, but his body cannot turn toward them.

After hearing it, the first wish still exists but temporarily loses its force. Odysseus now wants only to get closer. He has not compared all the consequences afresh or gained a new fact sufficient to overturn his earlier judgment. He has merely entered a moment he had already foreseen would change his choice.
So the crew's refusal to obey the command before them does not mean they deny the person before them.
They are carrying out the task that same person entrusted to them earlier.
This is a very particular kind of trust.
Odysseus has not handed every future decision over to the crew.
He has not said:
From now on, whenever you think my choice is dangerous, you may ignore me.
He delegates only a narrow piece of authority.
In these waters, while the song can influence him, before the ship has left the danger behind, they must not loosen his bonds even if he asks in person.
The place, danger, task, and condition for ending it are all clear.
That is precisely why this act of trust does not become a lasting takeover by others.
Once the ship has passed, the crew unties him. No one gains the standing to decide forever after when he is “not himself” merely because they were right not to obey him once.
This boundary matters.
There are many moments in life when we know our future selves may stop acting in the direction we currently endorse.
Some people put money somewhere they cannot easily access at any moment, knowing that immediate temptation can silence long-term plans.
Before things get worse, some ask a trusted person to keep an object, remind them of a promise, or activate an arrangement they have already agreed to when specified conditions arise.
Some write down a sentence:
If later I only want to run away, please remind me why I am choosing to continue now.
None of these practices necessarily means weakness.
Sometimes it is precisely by arranging things in advance that a person protects themselves from being wholly taken over by a passing moment.
But these arrangements remain their own choices not merely because they once said “I agree.”
It is also because that agreement has a scope and can specify when it ends.
Otherwise, Odysseus's method can easily become another dangerous story.
The past self might say:
At my clearest, I have already decided for the future. Whatever happens later, no change is allowed.
A promise can thus protect a direction, but it can also lock the future shut.
After all, our future selves are not always bewitched by Sirens.
They may also have learned facts their past selves did not know.
Someone once chose a line of work and only later saw the real cost of that life.
Someone promised to stay in one place forever, then found the conditions had changed completely.
Someone asked others to stop them giving up, but later wanted to stop not out of fear of difficulty, but because they finally understood that the original goal was not their own.
If every later change of mind is labeled “unreliable” in advance, the original promise becomes the past self's rule over the future.
So the truly difficult question is not “Do promises matter?”
It is this:
Does the later change come from a foreseen bout of temptation, or from new understanding?
How good were the past self's reasons to distrust judgment at a particular future moment?
On what grounds can the entrusted person know that the constraint still applies?
Does the future person have an opportunity to explain:
What is happening now is no longer the situation we originally agreed on?
Odysseus's story is so tidy precisely because the danger resembles a stretch of sea, with an entrance and an exit.
Real dangers often have no such clear boundaries.

This means entrusting someone in advance requires something more finely worked than ropes: explainable conditions, trustworthy people, a limited scope, and explicit preparations to restore the person's place as judge of their own affairs.
There is another difference in the story that is easy to overlook.
Odysseus has the crew plug their ears, but chooses to listen himself.
He does not merely want to avoid danger.
He also wants an experience his companions cannot have.
The crew must keep the course and do the work of bringing the ship through danger, yet they cannot hear the song. Odysseus enjoys the knowledge and gives them the task of protecting him.
This does not necessarily make his arrangement illegitimate.
He is the captain and has explained the method beforehand. If all the crew heard the song, no one aboard would be able to keep rowing.
But the story still leaves a question:
When someone chooses a dangerous experience for themselves, how much of the cost of protection can they hand to others?
If the arrangement fails, Odysseus at the mast will not be the only one to face destruction.
Every crew member will approach the Sirens with the ship.
Self-restraint appears to take place in one person, but in fact depends on a group untouched by the temptation keeping him on course.
So asking someone “Do not obey my future self” cannot be merely a private decision either.
That person needs to know what they are taking on, whether they can do it, and whether they are willing to become part of this constraint.
If an act of trust gives all the pressure to others but credits success only to one's own will, it still has not properly accounted for the relationship.
When the Sirens have finished singing, Odysseus has not proved himself stronger than desire.
He has even proved the opposite:
Under certain conditions, he knows he will change his commands.
What truly gets him through is not a heart that will never waver.
It is that, while still able to judge fully, he acknowledges he may later be unable to, and establishes a bounded relationship for that moment.
He temporarily entrusts part of his future to others.
They, in turn, do not use that trust to take possession of his future.
They refuse to listen when they should refuse, and let him go when they should let go.
Perhaps this is the hardest form of commitment.
It does not demand that the future obey the past forever.
Nor does it let every present pretend there was no past.
It enables the self at one moment to protect the self at another, while leaving the later self a door through which to regain judgment.
What the crew truly accomplishes is not merely binding Odysseus.
It is being willing to undo the ropes once the song has faded.

*Textual basis: Homer's Odyssey, Book XII. This essay follows the continuous account of Circe's warning about the Sirens, Odysseus's arrangement for the crew to stop their ears and bind him to the mast, and his orders to be released after hearing the song, to which the crew responds by tightening the ropes. The discussion concerns only the advance entrustment and limited constraint within this episode. It does not equate every change of mind with the Sirens' temptation.*
